assumptions.summary: Only 85% of 370 positions are filled and vacancies are placed evenly in low levels.
Churn is 18% annually and equal across levels; events occur monthly.
Affiliation is directed and unweighted; cooperation is undirected and weighted.
PAM position attributes persist or refresh according to the personnel event.
Training moves efficiency and churn through xi_1 and xi_2 toward stated baselines.
Low-level employees may leave directly while high-middle employees wait for substitutes.
Internal promotion has priority and follows seven levels without grade skipping.
Recruitment time is represented by a level-specific median and vacancies plan 2/3 recruitment.
The multilayer illustration uses 14 workers and three coupled layers.
Six runs and experience-based coefficients are sufficient for local sensitivity claims.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: ICM has 370 positions, seven levels, 85% working rate, salary ratio clues and supervisor-evaluated performance.
Monthly churn-rate definition, 18% baseline and 2/3 vacancy recruitment assumption.
Directed affiliation and weighted cooperation matrices with shortest-path intensity.
PAM attributes include level, salary, training/recruitment cost, churn, time, efficiency and on-job status.
Ten simulation traces for working rate, recruiting cost and training cost over 100 months.

language_observations.summary: The human style comes from concrete management pressure, explicit premise-to-recursion moves, event priority, curve mechanisms, policy tradeoffs, table recommendations, bounded error and final population limits.

the Summary turns a management brief into a network-to-policy route: Name the static graph, PAM, three event algorithms, budget and churn outputs, then close with multiplex and sensitivity boundaries.

an abstract human-capital concern becomes a team-management model: Open with intangible capital and team dependence, then move to the practical need to place trained people where their experience is useful.

partial occupancy and mid-level churn are converted into two concrete tasks: State the 85% occupancy, middle-level turbulence, salary and loyalty clues, then name the dynamic HCN and multilayer-network tasks.
a network-literature gap motivates a functional human-capital network: Move from natural and social network precedents to the practical gap of explaining churn and recruitment effects in teams.

fixed positions and missing employee detail trigger a Post Archives Matrix: Define positions rather than people as nodes, list the attributes that change with personnel events, and hand the archive to the dynamic model.

two relation semantics are separated before they are combined in performance: Distinguish directed affiliation from undirected, weighted cooperation, use matrices and shortest paths, and then combine them as team compactness.
training assumptions become state recursions: State the 85% fill, 18% churn, 2/3 recruitment and monthly timing assumptions, then update efficiency and churn through recovery coefficients.

a static productivity proxy hands off to three ordered personnel algorithms: Aggregate efficiency, base productivity and working time, then let demission, promotion, and recruitment change the PAM month by month.

a critical middle layer determines the order of the churn algorithm: Use monthly Monte Carlo churn, record a request, allow low-level departure, and route high-middle departure through promotion then recruitment.

vacancy eligibility hands a failed promotion to delayed recruitment: Check vacancies from the highest level, rank eligible service time, then record a recruitment plan in a time vector when no promotion fits.

curve shape is explained before the two-year budget is reported: Read the 85-to-80% working-rate path, attribute recruiting spikes to churn and training decline to staffing, then report 26.22 and 140.15 sigma.

same-axis churn scenarios turn trajectories into a staffing decision: Compare 25% and 35% against the baseline, read the below-80% crossing and final performance, and state the positive-feedback mechanism.

a policy comparison separates working rate from enthusiasm and mobility: Hold other parameters fixed, compare external versus internal middle-level recruitment, and admit that the better staffing policy can lower one subgroup's enthusiasm.

omitted everyday relations become layers and then graph statistics: Add friendship and competition to human capital, define node-layer coupling, and read density, path length and clustering into an HR data request.

a compact network table becomes a concrete organizational recommendation: Compare the four layer rows, notice the richer multilayer description and the dense competition layer, then recommend better data and team division.

random error is disclosed before coefficient changes are bounded: Repeat the working-rate simulation six times, define a signed error, then vary attenuation and churn-growth coefficients and retain a local stability claim.

broad modeling strengths are paired with explicit missing-network and missing-life limits: Claim PAM, dual relations, ordered algorithms and quantified abstractions, then admit omitted division operations and temporary/retired staff.

the conclusion restates the model as a sequence of handoffs: Close by repeating PAM, turnover/promotion/recruitment, revised scenarios, multiplex layers and sensitivity, without adding a new empirical claim.

a figure or table reading names the next reproducibility check: Quote the curve, layer row, algorithm branch or comparison that matters, then state the raw data, seed, edge list, threshold or fairness check still required.

results_trace.summary: Baseline working rate fluctuates around 85% for six months and stabilizes near 80% by month 100.
Ten traces average recruitment cost 26.22 sigma and training cost 140.15 sigma over two years.
At 25% churn working rate crosses 80% around month 12 and ends near 75%; at 35% it crosses around month 4 and ends near 67%.
Higher churn lowers performance toward about 179 sigma and 153 sigma and lowers enthusiasm toward 0.87 and 0.81.
Internal-only middle-level recruitment keeps working rate slightly higher and performance slightly higher.
After ten months external middle-level recruitment yields higher enthusiasm and more position changes.
The multilayer row has average degree 3.214, clustering 0.638, path length 1.571 and density 0.484.
Six-run signed stochastic error has maximum magnitude below 0.015.
Attenuation values above 0.93 and churn-growth values above 1.07 are reported as producing little visible change.
The final weaknesses omit division-operation effects and retirement or temporary absence.

source.title: Human Capital Dynamic Network Model of Team Science

source_quality.summary: All 22 physical pages were read in order twice and visually reviewed. The paper moves from 370-position PAM and two relation graphs through ordered personnel events, budget and churn-policy traces, a multilayer office, sensitivity checks and explicit population limits.

decisions: how positions are represented, how vacancies are filled, whether staffing sustains 80%, whether internal-only promotion is healthier, and what additional relation data are needed
inputs: 370-position hierarchy, 85% fill, 18% churn, affiliation/cooperation rules, PAM attributes, recruitment/training information, policy scenarios and multilayer office
outputs: static HCN, monthly event traces, productivity and budget proxies, churn-policy comparisons, multilayer statistics and sensitivity bounds

title: Human Capital Dynamic Network Model of Team Science
unresolved_questions: The Summary offers a complete network-to-policy story, but budget, occupancy and HR-health outputs remain internal simulation claims.
The 85% occupancy, middle-level churn and salary/loyalty clues are qualitative task inputs, not an observed longitudinal personnel dataset.
Churn-rate notation uses a monthly formula without fully stating units, while directed affiliation, shortest paths and alpha normalization lack disconnected-edge policy.
The cooperation compactness sum uses friendship intensity beta without a source, range, or empirical edge-strength calibration.
The seven-level allocation and evenly placed vacancies are presented as reasonable but are not validated against actual staffing.
Training recursions use xi coefficients and the fixed 18% baseline without fitting, bounds, seed, or a demonstrated relation between training and churn.
Productivity is a constructed proxy from efficiency, base productivity and working time; its units and observed business outcome are absent.
Monte Carlo churn is described as random, but probability assignment, seed, event order and high-middle boundary are not reproducibly frozen.
Promotion ranks working time and uses maximum productivity as eligibility, while tie handling, cross-division choice and threshold units are unspecified.
Recruitment assumes a median time, lowest-productivity hire and a vacancy-proportional plan without releasing rates, costs or raw event histories.

The baseline working-rate path fluctuates around 85% then stabilizes near 80%, and ten simulations report 26.22 sigma recruitment plus 140.15 sigma training, but cost provenance and uncertainty are missing.
The 25% and 35% paths cross below 80% by months 12 and 4 and end near 75% and 67%; this is a three-scenario simulation, not an external threshold test.
The no-external-recruitment comparison improves working rate slightly but lowers middle-level enthusiasm after month 10, exposing a policy tradeoff rather than a single best action.
The 14-person, three-layer network and adjacency tensor are illustrative; layer edges, cross-layer coupling and whole-company outcomes are not observed.
Table 1 reports internal degree, clustering, path length and density; the recommendation for more data and scientific team division is not a causal result.
Six-run stochastic error has maximum magnitude below 0.015, but the signed grouping formula, run count and no uncertainty propagation limit the claim.
Changing attenuation 0.90/0.93/0.95/0.97 and growth 1.05/1.07/1.10/1.13 yields local insensitivity claims without raw paths or a declared tolerance.
The strengths infer realistic quantification and common-sense agreement, while weaknesses omit division-operation networks and retirement/temporary absence.
The conclusion restates a complete workflow but adds no independent validation beyond the model's own simulations and illustrations.
